```{python}
#| label: agn-functions
#| include: false

# The course constants sheet, used by the dust figure on this page.
SIG = 5.6696e-5
WIEN = 2.89789e-1
PC, LD = 3.0856e18, 2.99792458e10 * 86400.0


def t_dust(L, r):
    """Temperature (K) of a blackbody dust grain a distance r (cm) from L (erg/s)."""
    return (L / (16 * np.pi * SIG * r**2)) ** 0.25
```

Lecture 18 met the quasars, the brightest of the black holes that are still
being fed, and lecture 19 went to the quiet one at the center of our own Galaxy.
Between those two extremes lies a whole family of galaxies whose centers are
lit by a growing black hole. Astronomers discovered the members of the family
one at a time, gave each a name, and for decades treated them as different
kinds of object. This lecture is about what is really there: one machine, seen
from different directions and run at different speeds.

## How to read this lecture

**These notes are the reading for this lecture, along with Kutner's §19.6.1,
*A common picture*** (about a page and a half, in the Chapter 19 PDF under
*Reading Material* in Canvas Files). The lecture builds one argument, and it is
worth holding onto from the start:

::: {.callout-important title="The idea at the center of this lecture"}
**Every active galactic nucleus has the same parts, and what we call one depends
mostly on the angle we see it from, how fast it is being fed, and whether it
has a jet.**
:::

*The spectrum of an active nucleus* shows that the light spans the whole
electromagnetic spectrum and that only part of it is the blackbody glow of
lecture 16's disk. *Where each part of the light comes from* builds the
machine, piece by piece, one piece for each part of the spectrum. *Accretion
rate and state* shows how the mix changes with the feeding rate. *The zoo and
the unified model* explains the names, and why most of them are one object seen
from different directions. *The dusty torus* does the arithmetic: how far out
the dust sits, and how much of the sky it hides.

## The spectrum of an active nucleus {#sec-spectrum}

An **active galactic nucleus**, or **AGN**, is the center of a galaxy where a
supermassive black hole is swallowing gas fast enough that the light from the
gas rivals or beats the light of the galaxy's stars. Quasars are the brightest
AGN. Lecture 16 predicted what such an object ought to look like: a disk of gas
at a range of temperatures, glowing like a stack of blackbodies, and nothing
else. Here is what one actually looks like.

:::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

Spread out the light of an AGN by frequency, from radio waves to gamma rays,
and you find five distinct features, each made by a different piece of the
machine:

1. **The big blue bump**, in the ultraviolet: the accretion disk of lecture 16.
   This is the part we expected, and it is only one part of the story.
2. **An infrared bump**: dust, a long way from the black hole, warmed by the
   disk's light and glowing in the infrared.
3. **A dip at about one micron** between those two bumps, called the
   **one-micron inflection**. It marks the boundary between the two sources of
   light, and we will see why it falls where it does when we get to the dust.
4. **A long flat stretch of X-rays**, reaching hundreds of keV, ending in a
   broad rise near 30 keV called the **Compton hump**.
5. **Radio emission** from electrons spiraling in magnetic fields. In most AGN
   this is faint. In a minority, roughly one in six among bright quasars, it
   is hundreds to thousands of times brighter, and those are the **radio-loud** AGN.

Every one of these is a clue. An ordinary star, or even a galaxy of them, puts
its light out in a narrow range of frequencies; an AGN spreads its light over
more than ten powers of ten in frequency. Most of it is not the disk's. Only a
small part of the spectrum is the thermal blackbody we would expect from an
accretion disk. And a piece of it can't be seen at all: hydrogen
gas in our own Galaxy absorbs nearly all of the extreme ultraviolet, right at
the top of the big blue bump, so the peak of the disk's light is usually
inferred rather than measured.

The shape is plotted in a way worth stopping to understand. Each horizontal
step on the plot is a factor of ten in frequency, and the vertical axis is
$\nu L_\nu$, which is the luminosity in that factor-of-ten range. So **the
height of the curve says directly where the energy is coming out**, and two
parts of the spectrum at the same height carry the same power. A flat stretch
means equal energy in every band. That is why this is the plot astronomers
reach for.

### Mathematical explanation

**What is plotted.** The luminosity per unit frequency is $L_\nu$, in
$\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$. Multiply it by the frequency and you get
$\nu L_\nu$, in $\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, a true luminosity. On a logarithmic
frequency axis, $\nu L_\nu$ is the power per unit $\ln \nu$:

$$
\int L_\nu \, d\nu = \int (\nu L_\nu) \, d\ln\nu .
$$ {#eq-nulnu}

Both sides have units of $\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, a luminosity, as they must,
since $d\ln\nu$ is a pure number. Equal heights therefore mean equal power in
equal logarithmic intervals, which is the point of the plot.

**Where the big blue bump sits.** Lecture 16 found the temperature of the disk,

$$
T(r) = \left( \frac{G M \dot M}{4 \pi \sigma r^3} \right)^{1/4} ,
$$

and showed that at a fixed number of Schwarzschild radii and a fixed fraction
of the Eddington rate it scales with the mass as

$$
T \propto M^{-1/4} .
$$ {#eq-t-scaling}

A disk around a $10\,M_\odot$ black hole, at its Eddington luminosity and at
the ISCO, reached $1.6 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}$ in lecture 16's worked
example. Scaling that to a black hole of mass $M$ gives

$$
T_{\mathrm{max}} = 1.6 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}
  \left( \frac{M}{10\,M_\odot} \right)^{-1/4} .
$$ {#eq-t-max}

A stellar-mass black hole's disk peaks in X-rays. A supermassive black hole's
disk, millions of times heavier, peaks in the ultraviolet, and that is the whole
reason for the name *big blue bump*.

**A sum of blackbodies.** The disk is not one temperature. Each ring radiates
like a blackbody at its own $T(r)$, so the disk's spectrum is the sum of many
Planck curves, the hot, small rings at high frequency and the cool, large rings
at low. That sum is what makes the bump broader than any single blackbody,
and it is what the code in the next tab adds up.

### Numerical exploration

@fig-sed builds an AGN spectrum out of its parts. The disk really is computed
by adding up rings at the temperatures of lecture 16's formula. The other
components are simple recipes with shapes chosen to match the observed spectra
[@elvis1994], so read the figure as a schematic of where each part sits, not as
a measurement. The code prints where the disk's own contribution peaks.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sed
#| fig-cap: "A schematic spectrum of an active nucleus, as $\\nu L_\\nu$ relative to the total luminosity $L$, against frequency on logarithmic axes, for a $10^{8}\\,M_\\odot$ black hole at its Eddington luminosity. The top axis gives the same frequencies as a wavelength or a photon energy. The disk (blue) is the sum of blackbody rings at the temperature of lecture 16; the dust (orange), the X-ray corona (green), the Compton hump (gray dashes) and the radio emission (gray dots) are simple recipes. The black curve is their sum. Radio emission is shown for a radio-loud nucleus and, much fainter, for a radio-quiet one."
#| fig-alt: "A chart with logarithmic axes. The horizontal axis is frequency from ten to the nine to ten to the twenty hertz, with a matching top axis marked 3 centimeters, 300 microns, 3 microns, 300 angstroms, 4 keV and 400 keV. The vertical axis is nu L nu relative to the total luminosity, from one millionth to about three. A solid black curve runs across the plot. At the left it starts at about one percent in the radio. It climbs steeply near ten to the twelve hertz into an orange infrared bump, flat at about one fifth from ten to the 13 to ten to the 14 hertz, dips to about one percent near ten to the 14.5 hertz, which is one micron, rises to a blue ultraviolet bump that peaks at about one half near ten to the 16 hertz, falls to about one percent in the X-rays where a green flat line runs, rises slightly at a gray dashed bump near 30 keV, and drops at the far right. A much fainter gray dotted line near one hundred thousandth marks a radio-quiet nucleus."
#| fig-height: 4.2

# Constants (cgs) from the course sheet.
C, G, H, KB, SIG = 2.99792458e10, 6.6732e-8, 6.6262e-27, 1.3806e-16, 5.6696e-5
MSUN, LEDD, ETA = 1.9891e33, 1.26e38, 0.057  # LEDD is per solar mass

M_bh = 1.0e8           # mass of the black hole, in solar masses
f_edd = 1.0            # luminosity as a fraction of the Eddington luminosity
cover = 0.5            # fraction of the sky covered by the dust

nu = np.logspace(9, 20.3, 1500)
dln = np.log(nu[1] / nu[0])
L = f_edd * LEDD * M_bh


def planck(nu, T):
    """The Planck function, up to a constant (the constant is normalized away)."""
    return nu**3 / np.expm1(np.minimum(H * nu / (KB * T), 600.0))


def scaled(L_nu, total):
    """Scale a spectrum so that it adds up to the luminosity `total`."""
    return L_nu * total / (L_nu * nu * dln).sum()


# The disk: rings from the ISCO to 100,000 r_S, at lecture 16's temperature.
rs = 2 * G * M_bh * MSUN / C**2
Mdot = L / (ETA * C**2)
r = rs * np.logspace(np.log10(3), 5, 200)
T = (G * M_bh * MSUN * Mdot / (4 * np.pi * SIG * r**3)) ** 0.25
disk = scaled((planck(nu[:, None], T) * r**2).sum(axis=1), L)

# The dust: equal energy per logarithmic step in temperature, 100 K to 1500 K.
T_d = np.logspace(2, np.log10(1500.0), 40)
dust = scaled((planck(nu[:, None], T_d) * nu[:, None] * T_d**-5.0).sum(axis=1),
              max(cover, 1e-9) * L)

# X-rays: a corona and the hump it makes by reflecting off the disk.
E = H * nu / 1.602e-9                               # photon energy in keV
corona = 0.02 * L * (E / 2.0) ** 0.1 * np.exp(-E / 300.0 - 0.1 / E)
hump = 0.006 * L * np.exp(-0.5 * (np.log10(E / 30.0) / 0.3) ** 2)

# Radio: a power law that turns over in the far infrared.
radio_loud = 0.005 * L * (nu / 5e9) ** 0.3 * np.exp(-nu / 1e12)
radio_quiet = 2e-3 * radio_loud

total = nu * (disk + dust) + corona + hump + radio_loud

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.55, 4.2))
ax.plot(nu, nu * disk / L, color=BLUE, lw=1.5, label="disk")
ax.plot(nu, nu * dust / L, color=ORANGE, lw=1.5, label="dust")
ax.plot(nu, corona / L, color=AQUA, lw=1.5, label="corona")
ax.plot(nu, hump / L, color=INK2, lw=1.3, ls="--", label="Compton hump")
ax.plot(nu, radio_loud / L, color=INK2, lw=1.3, ls=":", label="radio")
ax.plot(nu, radio_quiet / L, color=INK2, lw=1.3, ls=":")
ax.plot(nu, total / L, color=INK, lw=2.2, label="total")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1e9, 2e20)
ax.set_ylim(1e-6, 3.0)
ax.set_xlabel(r"frequency $\nu$ (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\nu L_\nu / L$")
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper left", ncol=2)
top = ax.secondary_xaxis("top")
top.set_xticks([1e10, 1e12, 1e14, 1e16, 1e18, 1e20])
top.set_xticklabels(["3 cm", r"300 $\mu$m", r"3 $\mu$m", r"300 Å", "4 keV", "400 keV"],
                    fontsize=9)
top.minorticks_off()
peak = nu[np.argmax(nu * disk)]
print(f"M = {M_bh:.0e} Msun, L = {L:.2e} erg/s")
print(f"disk peaks at {peak:.1e} Hz = {C / peak * 1e7:.0f} nm")
plt.show()
```

::::

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: where does the disk of a hundred-million-solar-mass black hole peak?"}
**The question.** A non-spinning black hole of $10^{8}\,M_\odot$ is shining at
its Eddington luminosity. How hot is its disk at the ISCO, and at what
wavelength does a blackbody at that temperature peak?

The scaling @eq-t-max carries the units along in the temperature it starts
from; the ratio of masses is a pure number. So

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{\mathrm{max}} &= 1.6 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}
  \left( \frac{10^{8}\,M_\odot}{10\,M_\odot} \right)^{-1/4} \\[0.8em]
 &= 1.6 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K} \times \left(10^{7}\right)^{-1/4} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The solar masses cancel. *Do the units make sense?* A kelvin in, and a pure
number multiplying it: a temperature, so yes. Now the number: $(10^{7})^{1/4} =
56$, so

$$
T_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}}{56}
  = 2.8 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{K} .
$$

Wien's law, on your constants sheet, gives the wavelength:

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{2.898 \times 10^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm\,K}}
  {2.8 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{K}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{cm} ,
$$

and the conversion to nanometers, set up so the unwanted unit cancels, is

$$
1.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{cm} \times
  \frac{10^{7}\ \mathrm{nm}}{1\ \mathrm{cm}} = 10\ \mathrm{nm} .
$$

The kelvins cancel, leaving a length. **The hottest part of the disk radiates at
about $10\ \mathrm{nm}$, in the extreme ultraviolet**, the band our own Galaxy's
hydrogen blocks. The whole disk's output adds up the cooler rings too, so the
bump as a whole peaks at a longer wavelength than this, as @fig-sed shows.
:::

## Where each part of the light comes from {#sec-parts}

@fig-unified, later in this lecture, is the whole machine in one picture. Here
we go through it one piece at a time, in order of distance from the black
hole.

### The disk

This is lecture 16's accretion disk: optically thick, geometrically thin, dense
and ionized, with the temperature falling with distance as $r^{-3/4}$. Its
inner edge is at the ISCO, its innermost rings reach hundreds of thousands of
kelvin around a supermassive black hole, and a large fraction of the energy is
released within a few tens of Schwarzschild radii. The idea that the big blue
bump is the thermal glow of such a disk goes back to 1978 [@shields1978]. The radiative efficiency
that comes out of this disk, the $\eta$ of lecture 7, is set by where the
ISCO is and so by the black hole's spin. That is the connection we have been
using since lecture 7, and it is why the big blue bump can be turned into a
statement about how much mass the black hole has swallowed.

### Magnetic fields and the corona

The disk is made of ionized gas, so the particles circulating in it are charged
particles in motion, and moving charges generate magnetic fields. The black
hole itself cannot do this: an isolated black hole, by the no-hair theorem of
lecture 2, has no magnetic field of its own. But a field can be induced in the
disk close to the hole, and the field lines are anchored to the disk by the
charged particles threading them. Lecture 16's magnetorotational instability
already told us that those fields are not a detail: they are the friction that
lets the disk accrete at all.

As the disk rotates, the field lines passing through it get wound up and
tangled. Anything wound up that tightly eventually snaps: two field lines
pointing in opposite directions touch, cancel, and reconnect in a new
configuration, releasing the energy stored in the field. This is **magnetic
reconnection**, and you have seen its effects. The photosphere of the Sun is
about $6000\ \mathrm{K}$, but its outer atmosphere, the corona, is at millions
of degrees, and the same process is thought to be responsible.

Around an accretion disk it is thought to do the same thing, on a grander
scale, and the energy released accelerates electrons to high energies. These
hot electrons form a tenuous cloud above and below the inner disk, named after
its solar counterpart: the **corona** [@haardt1991]. Lecture 16 used the corona
as the source of the X-rays that make the iron line. Now we can ask how it makes
them.

### X-rays: Compton scattering and its inverse

When a high-energy photon hits a free electron, it can bounce off, handing some
of its energy to the electron. This is **Compton scattering** [@compton1923].
The photon comes out with less energy, which is to say a longer wavelength, and
the shift depends only on the angle $\theta$ through which it was scattered:

$$
\Delta \lambda = \lambda' - \lambda
  = \frac{h}{m_e c} \left( 1 - \cos\theta \right) .
$$ {#eq-compton}

The combination $h/m_e c = 2.43 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm}$ is the **Compton
wavelength** of the electron. Check its units: $\mathrm{erg\,s}$ over
$\mathrm{g\,cm\,s^{-1}}$, with an erg being $\mathrm{g\,cm^{2}\,s^{-2}}$, gives
$\mathrm{cm}$, a length. The shift is tiny compared with the wavelength of
visible light and comparable to the wavelength of a hard X-ray, which is why
Compton scattering matters for X-rays and gamma rays and not for your reading
lamp.

**Inverse Compton scattering** is the same collision viewed from the other side.
A low-energy photon hits a fast-moving electron, and this time it is the
*photon* that gains energy, taken from the electron. For an electron with
Lorentz factor $\gamma$, a photon's energy goes up by roughly a factor of
$\gamma^2$.

This is how the corona works. The disk bathes it in ultraviolet photons. Those
photons run through the cloud of hot electrons, picking up energy as they
scatter, and leave as X-rays. In a real corona the electrons are at about a
billion kelvin, where their thermal energy is about a sixth of their rest
energy, so each scattering gives only a modest boost and it takes several scatterings to reach
the X-rays: the process is called **Comptonization**. The steady climb in
energy, one scatter at a time, is what produces the long flat stretch of X-rays
in @fig-sed. It cuts off where the photons have as much energy as the electrons
can give them, which is at hundreds of keV.

Some of those X-rays head back down and hit the disk. Most of them bounce off
it: this is the same Compton scattering, and the bounced X-rays pile up near
$30\ \mathrm{keV}$ to make the **Compton hump**. And some are absorbed by iron
atoms, which give off the iron line whose relativistic shape lecture 16
analyzed.

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: why the hump sits near 30 keV"}
**The question.** X-rays of $30\ \mathrm{keV}$ and of $300\ \mathrm{keV}$ each
scatter straight back off an electron in the disk ($\theta = 180°$). How much
energy does each keep?

A photon's wavelength is $\lambda = hc/E$. For the $300\ \mathrm{keV}$ photon,
with the energy converted to ergs,

$$
\begin{aligned}
E &= 300\ \mathrm{keV} \times
     \frac{1.602 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{erg}}{1\ \mathrm{keV}} \\[0.8em]
  &= 4.81 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{erg} , \\[0.8em]
\lambda &= \frac{6.626 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{erg\,s}
     \times 2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}}
     {4.81 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{erg}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The ergs and the seconds cancel, leaving centimeters. *Do the units make sense?*
A wavelength is a length, so yes. The number is
$\lambda = 4.13 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Straight-back scattering has
$1 - \cos\theta = 2$, so @eq-compton adds
$2 \times 2.43 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm} = 4.85 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda' &= 8.98 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm} , \\[0.8em]
E' &= 300\ \mathrm{keV} \times \frac{4.13}{8.98} = 138\ \mathrm{keV} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The $30\ \mathrm{keV}$ photon starts with a wavelength ten times longer,
$4.13 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm}$, and the same added shift takes it to
$4.62 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm}$, so it keeps
$30 \times 4.13/4.62 = 27\ \mathrm{keV}$. **The high-energy photon loses more
than half its energy, the low-energy one only a tenth.** So photons from high
energies pile down to the tens of keV, while below about $10\ \mathrm{keV}$ the
photons are absorbed by the disk's atoms instead of bouncing off. What is left
between those two limits is the hump.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about why the corona cannot make its X-rays on its own"}
Inverse Compton scattering does not create photons. It takes ones that already
exist and gives them more energy. So the corona needs a supply of low-energy
photons, and the disk underneath it provides them, in enormous numbers. A hot
electron cloud with nothing to scatter would stay dark.
:::

### Broad lines and narrow lines

Lecture 18 explained the **broad emission lines**: thousands of clouds of gas,
orbiting close to the black hole at thousands of kilometers per second, the
different speeds smearing each line out by the Doppler effect. That is the
**broad-line region**.

Much farther out, far beyond the dust we are about to meet, there is thinner
gas lit by the same ultraviolet light, moving only at hundreds of kilometers per
second. Its emission lines are correspondingly narrower. That is the
**narrow-line region**, and its lines are the second kind you will see in an
AGN spectrum.

### The dust

Beyond the broad-line region, at a fraction of a parsec to a few parsecs from
the black hole, gas is cool enough for dust grains to survive. The dust sits in
a thick, doughnut-shaped structure around the disk, called the **dusty torus**.
It absorbs the disk's ultraviolet light, gets warm, and re-emits that energy
in the infrared. That is **dust-reprocessed disk emission**, and it is the
infrared bump in @fig-sed. Dust cannot be heated without limit, as we will see
in the last section of this lecture, and that is what explains the one-micron
inflection.

### Radio emission and jets

The radio light comes from **synchrotron radiation**: relativistic electrons
spiraling around magnetic field lines, radiating as they go. In a radio-loud
AGN, most of it comes from **jets**, narrow streams of particles fired out along
the disk's axis, some of them reaching millions of parsecs. Jets are produced
when matter falling toward the black hole gets caught in the magnetic fields of
the inner disk, but how exactly, nobody yet knows for certain; Chapter 6 of the
textbook has some ideas. Lecture 22 is devoted to them.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-parts}

1. A $100\ \mathrm{keV}$ photon is Compton-scattered straight back
   ($\theta = 180°$). What is its new wavelength, and what is its new energy?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   Its wavelength goes from $1.24 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm}$ to
   $1.73 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm}$, and its energy from $100\ \mathrm{keV}$
   to $72\ \mathrm{keV}$.
   :::

2. If a single inverse Compton scattering multiplies a photon's energy by about
   $\gamma^2$, what Lorentz factor would an electron need in order to turn a
   $10\ \mathrm{eV}$ ultraviolet photon into a $1\ \mathrm{keV}$ X-ray in one
   scattering?

3. Gas orbiting a black hole of $10^{8}\,M_\odot$ moves at $5000\
   \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in the broad-line region and at $500\
   \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ in the narrow-line region. Use $r = GM/v^2$ (the
   enclosed-mass formula of lecture 17) to find how far each is from the black
   hole, in light-days or parsecs as seems natural.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   A factor of 10 in the speed is a factor of 100 in the radius. The broad-line
   gas is about $5.3 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm}$, or $20$ light-days, from the
   black hole, and the narrow-line gas is $5.3 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm}$, or

4. Explain in a sentence or two why a magnetic field in the disk is possible

   What does a black hole have to be like, by the no-hair theorem, and what is

:::

## Accretion rate and state {#sec-state}

The precise form of the spectrum depends on the accretion rate. Lecture 8
measured accretion rates in units of the Eddington rate, and the disk and the
corona respond to that number in opposite ways.

At **low accretion rates**, the inner disk is thought to be missing or puffed up,
and something hot above it, most likely a strong corona, dominates the X-rays. The photons that come
out are high in energy: this is called the **hard state**. At **high accretion
rates**, a bright disk runs close to the ISCO, the corona is weak, and the
X-rays are mostly low in energy: the **soft state**. Stellar-mass black holes
in X-ray binaries move between these states quickly enough for us to watch them
do it [@remillard2006]. The same physics in a supermassive
black hole would take far longer than a human lifetime, so we infer it by
comparing many AGN at different accretion rates rather than by watching one
change.

This is the second of the three things that decide what an AGN looks like, and
it tells us why a dim AGN and a bright one are not simply dimmed copies of one
another. Lower the accretion rate and the disk cools, since
$T \propto \dot M^{1/4}$ at a fixed radius, and the mix of the components changes too.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-state}

1. At fixed mass, the disk's temperature goes as $\dot M^{1/4}$. A black hole of
   $10^{8}\,M_\odot$ drops from its Eddington rate to one percent of it. By what
   factor does the temperature at the ISCO fall, and what does it become?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The factor is $(0.01)^{1/4} = 0.32$, so the temperature falls from
   $2.8 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{K}$ to $9.0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}$.
   :::

2. Imagine you are given the X-ray spectra of two black holes of the same mass
   and asked which has the higher accretion rate. What would you look for?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint"}
   Compare how much of the X-ray light comes out at high photon energy and how
   much at low.
   :::

:::

## The zoo and the unified model {#sec-unified}

AGN were discovered and named one kind at a time, by whatever instrument
happened to find them. So they carry a long list of names. The ones that matter
are few:

* **Quasars**: the brightest AGN, the subject of lecture 18.
* **Seyfert galaxies**: the same phenomenon in less luminous form, mostly in
  spiral galaxies, first catalogued by Carl Seyfert in 1943 [@seyfert1943].
  They come in two kinds. A **Seyfert 1** shows both broad and narrow emission
  lines in its spectrum. A **Seyfert 2** shows only narrow lines.
* **Radio galaxies**: the same phenomenon with relativistic radio jets, usually
  in giant elliptical galaxies, and usually with radio lobes far beyond the
  stars.
* **Blazars**: AGN whose brightness flickers violently and whose spectrum is
  dominated by a jet.

There are many more names in the literature, and most of them mark no real
difference. Blazars, BL Lacs, Fanaroff–Riley classes I and II [@fanaroff1974],
broad-line radio quasars, narrow-line Seyfert 1s: don't worry about these. The
important fact is that they are not all different animals.

### The picture

@fig-unified is the picture. A thick dusty torus surrounds the disk, the
broad-line region and the black hole. Look down the axis of the torus and you
see straight to the center: the disk's blue bump, the broad-line clouds and all
the rest. Look through the torus and the dust blocks everything inside it. What
you see then is only what is outside the torus: the narrow-line clouds, which
are far above it, the infrared glow of the torus itself, and hard X-rays, which
have enough energy to get through.

So **the difference between a Seyfert 1 and a Seyfert 2 is the angle we are
looking from.** A Seyfert 2 is a Seyfert 1 seen through its dust. Add a jet
to the same picture and the same geometry gives you the radio-loud sequence:
looking along the jet, you see a blazar; somewhat off the axis, a
broad-line radio galaxy or a radio-loud quasar; and through the torus, a
narrow-line radio galaxy.

```{python}
#| label: fig-unified
#| fig-cap: "The unified model of active galactic nuclei, in cross-section and not to scale. A thin accretion disk surrounds the black hole. The broad-line clouds sit close in, inside a thick torus of dust, with the narrow-line clouds far outside it. A jet leaves along the axis in a radio-loud object. An observer looking near the axis sees a type 1 AGN, with the broad lines visible; an observer looking through the torus sees a type 2 AGN; an observer looking straight down the jet sees a blazar."
#| fig-alt: "A cross-sectional diagram, not to scale. A small black circle at the center marks the black hole, with a thin horizontal blue accretion disk through it. Small gray clouds close to the center mark the broad-line region. A thick orange oval shape to the left and another to the right mark the torus of dust, with an opening above and below. Above the opening, farther out, a group of gray clouds marks the narrow-line region. A narrow gray jet extends upward and downward along the vertical axis. Three arrows point at the center from outside: from directly above, labeled blazar, along the jet; from about 30 degrees off the axis, labeled type 1, broad and narrow lines; and from the side through the torus, labeled type 2, narrow lines only."
#| fig-height: 4.3

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.3))
ax.set_xlim(-10, 10)
ax.set_ylim(-5.6, 7.2)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.axis("off")

# The torus, left and right, as thick ovals.
for x0 in (-5.6, 5.6):
    ax.add_patch(mpl.patches.Ellipse((x0, 0), 7.0, 4.4, fc=ORANGE, alpha=0.75,
                                     ec=INK, lw=0.8, zorder=2))
ax.text(-5.6, -3.0, "dusty torus", color=INK2, fontsize=10, ha="center")

# The jet, up and down the axis.
for s in (1, -1):
    ax.add_patch(mpl.patches.Polygon([(0, 0), (-0.45, s * 5.2), (0.45, s * 5.2)],
                                     fc=MUTED, alpha=0.6, ec="none", zorder=1))
ax.text(0.75, -5.0, "jet", color=INK2, fontsize=10, va="center")

# The accretion disk and the black hole.
ax.plot([-2.1, 2.1], [0, 0], color=BLUE, lw=3.2, zorder=4)
ax.add_patch(mpl.patches.Circle((0, 0), 0.22, fc=INK, ec=INK, zorder=5))
ax.text(2.4, -0.55, "disk", color=BLUE, fontsize=10, zorder=5)

# Broad-line clouds, close in; narrow-line clouds, far above the torus.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
ang = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, 24)
rad = rng.uniform(0.7, 1.6, 24)
ax.plot(rad * np.cos(ang), rad * np.sin(ang) * 0.7, "o", color=INK2, ms=3, zorder=3)
ax.text(-2.9, 3.1, "broad-line clouds", color=INK2, fontsize=10, ha="right")
ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.8, 0.9), xytext=(-2.7, 3.0),
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.8))
x_nlr = rng.uniform(-1.8, 1.8, 18)
y_nlr = rng.uniform(4.1, 5.5, 18)
ax.plot(x_nlr, y_nlr, "o", color=INK2, ms=4, zorder=3)
ax.text(-2.1, 5.2, "narrow-line\nclouds", color=INK2, fontsize=10, ha="right",
        va="center")


# Three sight lines, each from outside toward the center.
def sightline(angle_deg, length, text, ha, tx, ty, color):
    a = np.radians(angle_deg)
    xs, ys = length * np.sin(a), length * np.cos(a)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(0.25 * xs / length, 0.25 * ys / length), xytext=(xs, ys),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=color, lw=1.6), zorder=6)
    ax.text(tx, ty, text, color=color, fontsize=10.5, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=6)


sightline(2, 7.0, "blazar", "left", 0.75, 6.75, AQUA)
sightline(36, 8.2, "type 1: broad and\nnarrow lines", "left", 5.0, 6.4, BLUE)
sightline(83, 9.6, "type 2: narrow\nlines only", "right", 9.9, -3.2, INK)
plt.show()
```

The model has three parameters, and this is the central statement of the
lecture:

| what varies | what it does |
|:---|:---|
| **Viewing angle** | decides whether the dust hides the broad lines and the disk (type 1 or type 2), and whether the jet points at us (a blazar) |
| **Accretion rate** | decides how bright the object is and whether it is in the hard or the soft state |
| **Presence or absence of a jet** | decides whether it is radio-loud or radio-quiet |

### The evidence

The clearest evidence came from a clever trick. If a Seyfert 2 really is a
Seyfert 1 with its broad-line region hidden, some of the hidden light should
escape upward through the opening of the torus and scatter off gas above it
toward us. Scattered light is **polarized**, so a polarizing filter can pick it
out from the unpolarized glare. Robert Antonucci and Joseph Miller did exactly
this in 1985 with the Seyfert 2 galaxy NGC 1068, and in the polarized light its
spectrum looked just like a Seyfert 1's, broad lines and all [@antonucci1985].
The broad-line region was there the whole time, behind the dust.

Other evidence points the same way. Hard X-rays, which can get through the
torus, show Seyfert 2s to have the same central engines as Seyfert 1s, but
behind a large column of gas [@ramosalmeida2017]. And the narrow lines and the infrared glow from
the torus, which go out in every direction and are not blocked, are about the
same in both.

::: {.callout-warning .textbook-watch title="Textbook watch: is the unified model a hypothesis?"}
Kutner's §19.6 is headed *"A unified picture of active galaxies?"*, with the
question mark, and asks whether radio galaxies, Seyferts and quasars are
*"different manifestations of the same basic phenomenon."* That undersells it.
The orientation picture has been the
consensus since the early 1990s [@antonucci1993; @urry1995], and it is
essentially right: it accounts for most of the differences among AGN. It is
also not the whole story, as the next subsection says, but do not take the
book's question mark to mean that the matter is still open.
:::

### The part that is not orientation

The unified model explains about 95% of what is going on, which leaves a few
percent, and those few percent are where the action is now [@netzer2015].

**The torus is not a solid doughnut.** It is made of separate, dusty clouds
[@nenkova2008b], so a sight line near the edge of the torus has some chance of
passing through a gap. That turns the crisp line between type 1 and type 2 into
a probability.

**The covering fraction depends on the accretion rate.** In a large
X-ray sample, the gas covers about 85% of the sky around black holes below
roughly 3% of their Eddington rate, and only about 40% above it, because
radiation pressure on the dusty gas blows it out of the way [@ricci2017]. Orientation is therefore not the only thing
deciding what we see, and the same accretion rate that sets the spectrum also
reshapes the dust.

**Radio-loudness is not an orientation effect.** The presence of a jet is a
real physical difference between objects, and only 15 to 20 percent of bright
quasars are radio-loud [@kellermann1989]. Why some black holes launch powerful jets and
others do not remains an open question, with spin near the top of the list of
suspects.

**Some AGN change type on human timescales.** A *changing-look* AGN loses or
gains its broad lines within a decade or less [@lamassa2015], far too fast for a torus
to move across our line of sight. The source of the ultraviolet that lights up
the broad lines has simply dimmed or brightened. Unification is about what is
there; these objects remind us that what is lit up can change.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## The dusty torus {#sec-torus}

The picture has a number hidden in it. The dust glows because it is hot, and it
cannot be hotter than some limit. So we can ask how far from the black hole the
dust begins, and how much of the sky it hides.

:::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

A dust grain sitting in the disk's light absorbs what falls on it and warms up
until it radiates as much as it absorbs. Near the black hole there is more light
to absorb, so the grains get hotter, and at some distance they become so hot
that they evaporate. Dust grains, made of silicates and carbon, come apart at
about $1500\ \mathrm{K}$. That is why there is a hole in the middle of the
torus, why the broad-line region can exist inside it, and why the dust's light
stops at the near-infrared rather than going on into the visible.

A brighter nucleus pushes this edge outward: the amount of light falling on a
grain goes as $L/r^2$, so doubling the distance compensates for four times the
luminosity. The edge moves as the square root of $L$, and the dust around a
powerful quasar starts much farther out than the dust around a weak Seyfert.

The other number is the fraction of the sky the torus blocks. The disk's light
goes out in all directions and the torus intercepts whatever fraction falls on
it. The torus re-emits that energy in the infrared, so **the ratio of infrared
to ultraviolet luminosity measures how much of the sky the dust covers.** And
counting what fraction of AGN are type 2 measures the same thing another way,
since a type 2 is one seen through the dust.

### Mathematical explanation

**The temperature of a grain.** Take a dust grain of radius $a$, at a distance
$r$ from a source of luminosity $L$. It catches the source's light on its
cross-section $\pi a^2$, so it absorbs energy at the rate

$$
\frac{L}{4 \pi r^2} \, \pi a^2 ,
$$

and it radiates from its whole surface, of area $4 \pi a^2$, at the blackbody
rate $4 \pi a^2 \sigma T^4$. Setting these equal, the grain's size cancels:

$$
T^4 = \frac{L}{16 \pi \sigma r^2} .
$$ {#eq-dust-temp}

Check the units: $\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ over
$\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,K^{-4}\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^{2}}$ leaves
$\mathrm{K^{4}}$, as it should be. Notice that the size of the grain does not
appear: every grain at the same distance reaches the same temperature, which is
why this works at all.

**How far the dust begins.** Solve @eq-dust-temp for $r$, with $T$ set to the
temperature at which dust is destroyed, $T_{\mathrm{sub}} \approx
1500\ \mathrm{K}$ [@barvainis1987]:

$$
r_{\mathrm{sub}} = \sqrt{ \frac{L}{16 \pi \sigma T_{\mathrm{sub}}^{4}} } .
$$ {#eq-r-sub}

Real grains absorb ultraviolet light better than they radiate in the infrared,
so they run hotter than a blackbody at the same distance, and the real edge
is somewhat farther out than @eq-r-sub. It scales as
$r \propto L^{1/2}$ all the same, and the dust edge has been measured to do just
that [@suganuma2006].

**How much of the sky is covered.** Suppose the torus leaves open two cones
around the axis, each with half-opening angle $\theta$. The area of a spherical
cap of half-angle $\theta$ on a sphere of radius $R$ is
$2 \pi R^2 (1 - \cos\theta)$, a formula from solid geometry, so the two cones
together cover a fraction

$$
f_{\mathrm{open}} = \frac{2 \times 2 \pi R^2 (1 - \cos\theta)}{4 \pi R^2}
  = 1 - \cos\theta
$$ {#eq-open}

of the sky. A pure number, as a fraction should be. A randomly oriented AGN is
type 1 if we happen to lie inside the cones, so if the torus covers a fraction
$C = 1 - f_{\mathrm{open}} = \cos\theta$ of the sky,

$$
\frac{N_{\mathrm{type\,2}}}{N_{\mathrm{type\,1}} + N_{\mathrm{type\,2}}}
  = C = \cos\theta ,
$$ {#eq-cover}

and the torus's infrared luminosity is $L_{\mathrm{IR}} \approx C L$.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
{{< include ../../in_class/lec20/exercises00.qmd >}}
:::

### Numerical exploration

@fig-dust plots @eq-dust-temp for two AGN, one a hundred times brighter than the
other. Dust cannot exist where the curve is above $1500\ \mathrm{K}$, so the
place where each curve crosses that line is the inner edge of its torus.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dust
#| fig-cap: "The temperature of a blackbody dust grain against distance from a nucleus of luminosity $10^{44}$ and $10^{46}\\ \\mathrm{erg\\,s^{-1}}$, on logarithmic axes. Above $1500\\ \\mathrm{K}$ dust is destroyed, so no dust exists in the shaded band. Each curve crosses that line at the inner edge of its torus, which moves out as the square root of the luminosity. The right-hand scale is the wavelength at which a blackbody of that temperature peaks."
#| fig-alt: "A chart with logarithmic axes. The horizontal axis is distance from the black hole, from a thousandth of a parsec to a hundred parsecs. The vertical axis is dust temperature from about 30 to 10,000 kelvin, with a right-hand axis giving the peak wavelength of a blackbody at that temperature, from about 0.3 to about 100 microns. Two straight lines fall from upper left to lower right. The blue line for a luminosity of 10 to the 44 is below the orange line for 10 to the 46. A shaded band covers everything above 1500 kelvin. The blue line reaches 1500 kelvin at about 0.03 parsecs and the orange at about 0.3 parsecs, each marked with a dot."
#| fig-height: 4.2

r_pc = np.logspace(-3, 2, 200)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.55, 4.2))
ax.axhspan(1500, 1e4, color=ORANGE, alpha=0.12, zorder=0)
ax.axhline(1500, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.1, zorder=1)
ax.text(0.7, 1800, "too hot: dust is destroyed", color=INK2, fontsize=10)
for L, col, tag in ((1e44, BLUE, r"$L = 10^{44}$ erg/s"),
                    (1e46, ORANGE, r"$L = 10^{46}$ erg/s")):
    ax.plot(r_pc, t_dust(L, r_pc * PC), color=col, lw=2.2, zorder=3, label=tag)
    r_edge = np.sqrt(L / (16 * np.pi * SIG * 1500.0**4))
    ax.plot([r_edge / PC], [1500.0], "o", color=col, mec=INK, mew=0.7, ms=7, zorder=4)
    print(f"L = {L:.0e}: dust begins at {r_edge / PC:.3f} pc "
          f"= {r_edge / LD:.0f} light-days")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(1e-3, 100)
ax.set_ylim(30, 1e4)
ax.set_xlabel("distance from the black hole (pc)")
ax.set_ylabel("dust temperature (K)")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=9.5)
right = ax.secondary_yaxis("right", functions=(lambda T: WIEN / T * 1e4,
                                               lambda lam: WIEN / lam * 1e4))
right.set_ylabel(r"peak wavelength ($\mu$m)")
plt.show()
```

The right-hand scale shows why the one-micron inflection is where it is. Dust
at the sublimation temperature of $1500\ \mathrm{K}$ peaks at about
$2\ \mu\text{m}$ and has a falling spectrum shortward of that, and no dust is
hotter. The disk's light, climbing toward the ultraviolet, has its long-wavelength
tail there. Somewhere between them is a minimum, and it falls near one micron.
It is not a feature of any one thing; it is the gap between two.

::::

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: the inner edge of a Seyfert's torus"}
**The question.** A Seyfert nucleus has a luminosity of
$10^{44}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. Treating dust grains as blackbodies, how far
from the black hole can dust survive at $1500\ \mathrm{K}$?

From @eq-r-sub, with the units attached. On the bottom,

$$
\begin{aligned}
16 \pi \sigma T^4 &= 16 \pi \times 5.67 \times 10^{-5}\
    \mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,K^{-4}\,s^{-1}} \\[0.8em]
    &\quad \times \left(1500\ \mathrm{K}\right)^4 .
\end{aligned}
$$

The $\mathrm{K^{4}}$ cancels, leaving $\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$. Dividing
$\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ by that leaves $\mathrm{cm^{2}}$, and its square root is
$\mathrm{cm}$. *Do the units make sense?* A distance, so yes. Now the numbers:
$16 \pi \sigma T^4 = 1.44 \times 10^{10}$, so

$$
r_{\mathrm{sub}} = \sqrt{ \frac{10^{44}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}}
  {1.44 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,s^{-1}}} }
  = 8.3 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm} .
$$

In light-days, with a conversion fraction arranged so the unwanted unit cancels,

$$
8.3 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm} \times
  \frac{1\ \text{light-day}}{2.59 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm}}
  = 32\ \text{light-days} .
$$

**About a month of light-travel time.** The actual dust edge of a Seyfert of this
brightness is measured by watching the infrared follow changes in the disk's
light, and it lies at tens of light-days [@suganuma2006], a success for one line
of arithmetic.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about what the type 2 fraction says about the torus"}
Suppose exactly half of AGN of some luminosity are type 2. From @eq-cover,
$\cos\theta = 1/2$, so $\theta = 60°$: the dust covers the part of the sky within
$30°$ of the plane of the disk. Measuring the ratio of types is measuring a
shape. And since $L_{\mathrm{IR}} \approx C L$, the infrared to ultraviolet
ratio in a single object measures the same thing again, independently. In a
sample of nearby Seyferts, type 2 outnumber type 1 by about 4 to 1
[@maiolino1995], which would make $\cos\theta = 0.8$ and $\theta = 37°$.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-torus}

1. Use @eq-r-sub to find how far dust begins around a quasar with
   $L = 10^{47}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. Give the answer in centimeters and in
   parsecs.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   $2.6 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm}$, or $0.85\ \mathrm{pc}$.
   :::

2. A nucleus dims by a factor of 100 and stays dim. Where does the inner edge of
   the torus eventually go, relative to where it was?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   In by a factor of 10, since $r_{\mathrm{sub}} \propto L^{1/2}$.
   :::

3. At what temperature is a dust grain $1\ \mathrm{pc}$ from a nucleus of
   $L = 10^{46}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, and where does its blackbody spectrum
   peak?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   Use @eq-dust-temp, and take the fourth root last. The temperature is about
   $780\ \mathrm{K}$, and the peak is at about $3.7\ \mu\text{m}$.
   :::

4. Survey counts show that $40\%$ of the AGN of some luminosity are type 1. What
   is the half-opening angle of the cones, assuming every torus has the same
   shape?

5. A nucleus of $10^{45}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ has a torus covering $60\%$ of
   its sky. How much infrared luminosity do you expect from the dust?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   $L_{\mathrm{IR}} \approx 6 \times 10^{44}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$.
   :::

:::

## If you want to go further

None of this section is needed for what comes before or after.

**Kutner, §19.2 and the rest of §19.6.** The chapter PDF in Canvas Files has a
good qualitative account of radio galaxies (§19.2), and §19.6.2 turns to the
hunt for supermassive black holes in the nuclei of nearby galaxies, which is
where lecture 21 begins.

**The reviews.** Antonucci's 1993 review [-@antonucci1993] and Urry and
Padovani's 1995 review [-@urry1995] are the two that made unification the
standard picture, and both are readable. Netzer's 2015 review [-@netzer2015] is
the state of the art, with a clear view of what the model does not explain.

## Summary

| idea | result | why it matters |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Spectrum | five components, plotted as $\nu L_\nu$ | only one is the disk's blackbody |
| Big blue bump | $T \propto M^{-1/4}$; a $10^{8}\,M_\odot$ disk reaches $2.8 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{K}$ at the ISCO | why supermassive black holes shine in the ultraviolet |
| Corona | magnetic reconnection heats electrons above the disk | a hot cloud that needs the disk's photons |
| X-rays | Compton scattering, $\Delta\lambda = (h/m_e c)(1 - \cos\theta)$, and its inverse | UV photons become X-rays; X-rays reflect to make the Compton hump |
| Dusty torus | reprocessed disk light, in the infrared | hides what is inside it |
| Radio | synchrotron from jets | present only in the minority that are radio-loud |
| State | hard at low $\dot M$, soft at high $\dot M$ | the spectrum depends on the feeding rate |
| Unified model | viewing angle, accretion rate, jet | most of the zoo is one machine |
| Dust edge | $r_{\mathrm{sub}} = \sqrt{L/16\pi\sigma T^4}$ with $T \approx 1500\ \mathrm{K}$ | the torus has a hole in it, sized by $L$ |
| Covering | $C = \cos\theta$ and $L_{\mathrm{IR}} \approx C L$ | counting types and measuring the infrared both measure the shape |

An active galactic nucleus is one machine with many names. The disk makes the
ultraviolet, the corona turns some of it into X-rays, the dust turns more of it
into the infrared, a jet may or may not carry energy out along the axis, and
where we happen to be standing does the rest. Next time we step back from the
machine to ask about the galaxy around it: why the mass of a black hole, a tiny
fraction of its galaxy's, should be so closely tied to the galaxy it lives in.
